     "subtitle": "Travel as an investment: instead of in bricks, in the daughters' experiences",
     "screenshot_description": "Vedran Soric and Zoran Salopek at a table at the start of the conversation, the host explaining why they traveled with their daughters.",
     "content": "The episode begins with a short introduction in which the host **Vedran Soric** admits that the conversation with the guest, **Zoran Salopek**, started so spontaneously that he almost forgot to greet the viewers and listeners. Zoran Salopek points out that precisely the repeated question from the beginning of the conversation was excellent and that everyone can learn from it. The question referred to the experiences and travels that Vedran Soric provided for his daughters.\n\nVedran Soric explains that he and his wife, as parents, decided to enable their daughters to travel „really a lot“, instead of investing money in „bricks“ and similar things. That decision, as he says, was actually an investment in the daughters, in such a way that they would experience as much of life as possible. Salopek logically adds that the question also imposes itself of who invested in them themselves.\n\nThe host replies that he himself began traveling very early because his job required it of him. His 15 years of work in sales were, as he says, 15 years on the road. Salopek concludes that this meant a great broadening of perspective and that Vedran Soric wanted to pass on to his daughters what he had learned. The guest adds that he himself did exactly the same with his daughters, but that time showed that there is also another side to the story.",

     "subtitle": "A lesson about peace: „Today we are not going anywhere and we are not doing anything“",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek tells about the day he told his daughters that they were not going anywhere today.",
     "content": "Zoran Salopek reveals why time did not confirm that „everything together“ worked. One day he heard his daughter's sentence: „What are we going to do today?“ In that simple sentence he heard, as he says, the whole universe. He recognized a constant restlessness: where are we going today, what are we doing today, what will we amuse ourselves with, what has dad come up with today. At the same time, in that question he also saw a lot of love toward himself as a father.\n\nThat day he decided: **„Today we are not going anywhere and today we are not doing anything.“** They could play basketball and spend time together. What the children needed to learn on trips and in amusement parks, he judged, had already been completed. A border was being crossed where all of it began to be taken for granted and normal, and with it came restlessness.\n\nSalopek emphasizes that restlessness in itself is not a problem. His daughter's question nevertheless reflected to him the state of awareness. When they all „did nothing“ together, they found, he says, a great connection and closeness which they had lost while running after experiences. He concludes that until then dad had been teaching his daughters how to start, and that with mom he had to learn also how to stop.\n\nThat applies personally, and in business, and privately, and in parenting. He speaks about balance: whenever he notices an imbalance, he tries to return it to the middle, both in himself and in others.",

     "subtitle": "Prejudices and assumptions: two traps of sales, one root",
     "screenshot_description": "The host asks a question about the difference between prejudice and assumption, the guest answering while listening.",
     "content": "**Vedran Soric** opens a new topic: misunderstanding and assumptions are two big problems in business, especially in sales. Since the guest deals with the meaning of terms, he asks him what the difference is between prejudice and assumption. **Zoran Salopek** explains that terminology is important to him, among other things because of writing books, since he wants to give people clarity, and for that he himself first needs clarity.\n\nThe host refers to a recent post on LinkedIn whose author he apologizes to for not being able to name. In it, it was stated that prejudices in sales are much more dangerous than assumptions. A salesperson has the right to assume that something will or will not happen, but must not have a prejudice. Vedran Soric says that the thought was excellently phrased.\n\nSalopek nevertheless claims that more important than terminology itself is that for the sake of which we study it: **understanding**. It is precisely that, he says, the reason why we are here in life. Understanding is the same in sales, in private and in business life, because it is about the same person. We separate them only in the head.\n\nThe guest concludes that assumptions and prejudices come from the same root, and that is **our inability to admit that we do not know something**.",

     "subtitle": "The courage to say „I don't know“: a sign of maturity, not of weakness",
     "screenshot_description": "Vedran Soric talks about the first time he admitted in front of training participants that he did not know something.",
     "content": "Zoran Salopek immediately applies his own thesis in practice. When the host asked him something that he did not know at that moment, he could have started to fumble, but he correctly said: „I don't know.“ He warns about the irony: „the great Zoran“, who constantly talks about wisdom on numerous podcasts, says that he does not know in the same podcast. He considers that this is how one learns by example, because in parenting, sales, leadership and everything else the one who leads is the one who first shows his own ignorance and weakness, and says: „I don't know, but I will find out“. The guest emphasizes that because of this he does not feel lost or unimportant.\n\nVedran Soric shares a personal experience. Five years ago at a training he said „I don't know“ to the participants for the first time. A silence fell, and he added that he could look it up during the break, but that he really does not know. He admits that it sounds silly, but that afterward he felt lighter.\n\nSalopek replies that this is not silly, but **the whole meaning of life**. He emphasizes that strength and courage were needed for the admission and that this maturity must be acquired. The relief that the host felt, the guest describes as the feeling we have when we do something right.\n\nThe host adds that over time he went a step further. To some questions he says that he does not know and that it does not even interest him, and that he will not research it because it is not important for what he does. Salopek calls this **maturity and awareness**: to accept ignorance and uncertainty and to be at peace with it.",
     "keywords": [
      "ignorance",

      "courage",

     "subtitle": "Opinion has no responsibility, knowledge has a first and last name",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek explains the difference between opinion and knowledge with gesturing.",
     "content": "To the question of why people are afraid to say that they do not know, Zoran Salopek replies that the reason is simple: they lose the **feeling of importance**. People want to be seen, heard and important, and the reason for that, he claims, is the feeling that they are insufficient and lacking to themselves. They do not understand themselves, so they seek from others what they themselves do not have. When he understood that regularity, he no longer dared to state his opinion lightly, but tried to speak from knowledge, because **opinion and ignorance do not go in the same sentence**.\n\nThe host asks how to draw a clear difference between opinion and knowledge. The guest says that it is very clear:\n\n- **Knowledge is complete responsibility.** When he claims that he knows something, he says it with his first and last name, he does not hide behind philosophy, religion, courses or other people's names. He says: „I know this, I teach this and I show it with my own life“.\n- **Opinion carries no responsibility.** The sentence „I think you should“ easily turns into „I only gave my opinion“.\n\nSalopek claims that the whole universe revolves around responsibility. He recalls conversations with serious business people who had top ideas, but who broke down on the same thing: they would have to come out with their first and last name, without the protection of a firm, a corporation and money. When he told them to put their face on a poster and present the idea, their personality, he says, would fall apart. The ability to be alone in your own burdens, struggles and in expressing what you are, he concludes, is **the path to freedom**.",
     "keywords": [
      "opinion",
      "knowledge",
      "responsibility",
      "feeling of importance",

     "screenshot_description": "The host and the guest talk about sales and payment collection, the host emphasizing „money in the account“.",
     "content": "When the guest mentions responsibility, **Vedran Soric** says that in sales it is like a forgotten skill. When a salesperson tells him that he sold, he always asks: „And is the money in the account?“ The answer is often: „No, but I finished that.“ **Zoran Salopek** immediately replies that he did not finish because he did not collect payment. Responsibility, he emphasizes, ends only with the money in the account. The host adds that then a new responsibility begins: repeat purchase.\n\nSalopek then asks whether this is a question of leadership and management or only of sales, or whether it also holds in the family. He concludes that it is about **the same person on all platforms**. The host follows up on the claim „at home I am much calmer“, to which the guest says that one should also ask the household members whether that is true and what they would say.\n\nVedran Soric retells a recent training at which one participant claimed that she is a different person at home than at work. He suggested to her that a personality test be filled out by her colleague from work, and that someone from her home also fill it out, for example her husband, and that the results then be compared. The results turned out the same. The host interprets this as proof that the perspective from the other side shows what we really are in relation to what we think we are.",

     "content": "Zoran Salopek poses a question which is, he says, key: are people at all interested in what they really are like, or do they want to remain convinced that they are the way they see themselves. **Vedran Soric** agrees that people often ask in order to get an answer that they already have.\n\nThe guest presents his own experience: out of ten questions that he receives, **eight people ask in order to confirm what they already think**, and only two are sincere, motivated by „childlike curiosity“ and a readiness to truly learn something. In those eight, people are actually saying: „Just tell me what I have in my head as truth.“\n\nThe host connects that thought with the topics of the conversation: consistency and childlike curiosity. A top salesperson, he emphasizes, must be curious because from curiosity arises the desire to help someone and to fully understand what he needs.      "content": "Zoran Salopek claims that most of the people he talks with he must first teach to stop talking and to listen to the interlocutor. The salesman talked and talked, and Salopek told him that perhaps it was time to stop talking, to show the product on the faucet and to take a screwdriver. The salesman replied that he did not know how to do that, but then continued to explain that he would save 50 percent of the water.\n\nIn the meantime the guest calculated himself that the saving would be 25, and not 50 percent. He told the salesman that 25 percent was a phenomenal saving and that he would buy everything. Salopek thus **sold the product to himself in two seconds**, because he saw that the salesman was going into excessive explaining instead of into demonstration.      "subtitle": "The confused customer and the power of silence",
     "screenshot_description": "The host and the guest talk about silence in a sales conversation and public speaking.",
     "content": "**Vedran Soric** knows in sales the expression „confused customer“: a customer is lost when the salesperson explains too much. When he buries someone with everything he knows, the person feels inferior, as if he is not worth as much as the salesperson, who knows so much about the product. Then, he says, something arises, perhaps ego, and the customer does not buy not because he does not need the product, but because he thinks: „Well now I definitely won't.“ **Zoran Salopek** calls this spite.\n\nThe guest returns to the example with the water adapters. He knows what drove the salesman to excessive talking: his silence. He was silent out of love, to give him space to say what he had, but the salesman misinterpreted the silence, did not know how to deal with uncertainty and began to speak too much. The point, says Salopek, is in the skill of knowing how to remain in silence, discomfort and peace. That skill can also be a **perfect sales tool** and can be used as manipulation.\n\nThe host confirms that this is very hard for people. He suggests a simple experiment at the first call: say „Good day, I am so-and-so“ and fall silent. It will be seen how powerful that is. Salopek adds that the same holds in public speaking, where the pause is key, but two seconds of silence seem to the speaker like two minutes.",

     "subtitle": "Say „no“ without justification: consistency as the foundation of trust",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek explains how he taught employees to say „no“ to clients without justification.",
     "content": "Zoran Salopek talks about an experience from twelve years of running a firm, during which about a hundred employees passed through it. To numerous irrational client demands he did not find a single person who knew how to simply say „no“. A justification always came: „I'll ask the boss“ or „I'll have a look.“ His answer was: don't ask the boss, you have clear rules, just say no. Example: a client asks whether he can have a discount after he has slept in the property, and the answer should be no, **without justification and unconditionally**.\n\nWhen they asked him what that would look like, he showed an example. To the question „Can I have a discount?“ the answer is „No“, and if the client says „No problem“, he pays and leaves. He applies the same rules with children. If a child asks whether he may have chocolate before dinner and the answer is no, he must not ask a second time. Vedran Soric calls this **consistency**: children must learn that „no“ means „no“.\n\nSalopek describes consistency as one of the many skills that we must carry: do what you say. When he was choosing builders for his properties, one of the biggest criteria was that the contractor **picks up the phone every time** and does what they agreed. He is ready to pay a higher price because he knows that a consistent person takes responsibility and answers for his work. Even when the deadline shifts, he knows that the person will communicate clearly, that he will not run away or become aggressive.",

     "subtitle": "Replaced brakes and a culture of error analysis",
     "screenshot_description": "Vedran Soric retells the case with a car repair shop and the replacement of brake discs.",
     "content": "**Vedran Soric** illustrates consistency and responsibility with an example from a car repair shop. On the car, all four discs and all the pads had to be replaced. He picked it up, signed, paid and left. Already after a few days he noticed a slight shaking of the steering wheel, and after a week, when it did not stop, he looked at the wheels and saw that **the front discs had not been replaced**.\n\nHe called the mechanic and sent photographs. The mechanic called back in about twenty minutes and said that he did not know how that had happened. Afterward it turned out that somewhere in the chain communication had failed: the discs had arrived the same twice, so they were returned to the supplier. The mechanic apologized, admitted that this was now a problem for Vedran because he had to bring the car again, and offered to sort out his car in one day. There was no aggression or shifting of blame.\n\nThe host emphasizes that anyone can slip, but the problem is the absence of a **culture of communication about mistakes**. He refers to a colleague from aviation who had previously appeared on the show: in the military every mistake is analyzed down to the smallest detail, because that is the only way for it not to be repeated, especially when the same mistake in a helicopter could cost the life of an inexperienced pilot. **Zoran Salopek** adds that the military and Toyota do the same in production processes.",

     "subtitle": "Self-questioning and truth: the brain always first offers an excuse",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek explains metacognitive self-questioning and truth as the common denominator of all techniques.",
     "content": "**Zoran Salopek** talks about a technique that he advocates, and it is called **metacognitive self-questioning**. In the world, he says, there are more than 30 thousand spiritual, religious, philosophical and psychological techniques of self-improvement, and what runs through all thirty thousand is **truth**. He deals with truth and love, and his wife told him that he is the only one who can make a business out of love and truth. Love is truth, and they have no direction, technique or religion of their own: they are themselves the direction.\n\nThe guest connects this with what the host said about the military. They arrive at truth through the mistake and look for the **cause, not the consequence**. They do the same in the production process: when something goes wrong, they do not stop at the first thing that happened, but ask „why?“. In our mind this is called self-questioning: asking the question „why“ five times. In doing so one asks: why am I reacting, is this my defensive mechanism?\n\nSalopek warns that our brain will always first give us an excuse and a justification. In sales and management this is an automatism. The question is whether someone will live with that excuse, although everyone around him knows that he made a mistake. Admission is everyone's right, but someone will walk around with that energy and with the financial and business results that the inability to admit one's own mistake brings. Therefore the guest concludes that it is everyone's responsibility to find his own mistake himself.",
     "keywords": [
      "self-questioning",
      "truth",
      "love",
      "cause and consequence",
      "excuse"

     "subtitle": "Guilt is not responsibility, and „so what?“ stops the inventing of excuses",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek emphasizes the difference between guilt and responsibility.",
     "content": "When the host, speaking about a sales team leader and a poor performer, says that the problem is „in you“, he corrects himself mid-sentence and turns it into „your responsibility“. **Zoran Salopek** catches that difference: **guilt and responsibility are not the same**.\n\nThe guest claims that the only reason he succeeded in business is that he did not look at who is to blame, but whose responsibility it is. He is not to blame for the problems that arose, but it is his responsibility to solve them. The same holds for the owner of the repair shop from the previous example: he is not to blame for the mistake of someone in the system, but he is responsible and that is why he called and said that he would sort it out. Salopek transfers this to the whole of life: he is not to blame for his childhood or for tax problems, but it is his responsibility to solve them.\n\nThat state, when you realize that you alone are responsible for everything (for life, emotions, results, place in society and career), the guest calls **loneliness**. He warns that people compare themselves and say „it's easy for him, he has rich parents“, but they do not see the whole picture because they look only from the outside.\n\nFor this he has a technique that he teaches people: the question **„So what?“**. When someone comes to him with a thousand justifications, the answer is „so what“. Even more important: he will not invent excuses for himself. Vedran Soric admits that this is very hard and that he himself used to invent excuses. To Salopek's question of whether because of this he understands more the people who lie, he replies that he understands more than before. Everyone has been through it, and probably no one can get rid of it completely.",

     "subtitle": "Listen to what you say: the subconscious, automatisms and arrogance",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek explains the technique of listening to one's own words and the subconscious.",
     "content": "Salopek offers a very simple technique of checking oneself: **listen to what you say**. The subconscious, he claims, people excessively mystify. We have only about five percent of the conscious part, and the rest are automatisms that act without thinking. What we say by automatism comes out of the subconscious and shows what is truly in our head.\n\nThe guest cites his own example. On one podcast they asked him what could throw him out of balance, and he answered „nothing“. He recognized that that statement was **arrogance that came out of him**. He admits that arrogance still sometimes slips out of him, because the point is not to be perfect, but to be aware enough to listen to yourself while you talk. When you are aware enough, the words, as he says, „scratch your ears“. He concludes: the automatism exists, but it does not give him power.\n\nSalopek here speaks about arrogance and the need to apologize in that context. The point is not to eliminate all mistakes, but to **notice them at the moment while they are happening** and not let them determine behavior.",

     "subtitle": "„Society does not exist“: responsibility is always personal",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek claims that society does not exist, the host listening with interest.",
     "content": "**Vedran Soric** asks whether the fact that we predominantly communicate via keyboard and audio messages, so that we first think and only then respond, is not slowing down today's society. **Zoran Salopek** answers briefly: **„Society does not exist.“** The host describes this as an interesting answer.\n\nThe guest explains that this is the same automatism he spoke about: we all gladly hide behind „society“. When he talks with a woman, there is no „woman“, but one concrete person. Nor do „we salespeople“ exist, there is an individual. That is why he constantly emphasizes responsibility and the ability to be alone, because „there is no us“. We all have the right to say whatever we want about society, but the question is how it goes in practice.\n\nSalopek then touches on blanket advice. We all like to give it, but it is not wise, because what holds for one can be completely the opposite for another. People come from different perspectives: they climb the same mountain from different sides, and what is a weakness for one is a strength for another. The book he is currently writing is precisely about wisdom.",

     "subtitle": "Technology is not to blame: everything is neutral, the difference is in us",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek explains how he teaches children to use technology without demonizing it.",
     "content": "The guest continues the thought about wisdom with the example of technology. For a person who is deeply convinced that technology is to blame for all the evil of the world, strength would be to understand technology and its place in the evolution of society. Nothing can be **rejected or accepted a priori**. Wisdom is to understand why something exists at all and to find balance in using it.\n\nHis children, says **Zoran Salopek**, he will not teach that technology is to blame, but he will not teach them to spend hours on it either. He will teach them to use it, take what they need, say „enough“, draw a line and move on without it. To claim that something is a priori bad or wrong is not wise, because **everything in the universe is neutral**. **Vedran Soric** agrees that we attribute meaning to it.\n\nSalopek emphasizes that the same holds for manipulation, theft and cheating. Everything is neutral, and what defines us is why we do something: out of weakness or out of strength.",

     "subtitle": "Theft from the cash register: what would love and truth do?",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek tells about the case of an employee who stole money from the cash register.",
     "content": "As a concrete example Salopek cites a case from the past. One employee stole money from the cash register, and another discovered it and told him. He asked himself what **love and truth** would do in that situation.\n\nFirst they would remain calm and wait. Two minutes before reacting they would not allow impulsiveness, but would think. Then they would look for the motive, and in order to find it out, he must admit that he does not know it. That is why he confronted her with the question: why did this happen? Then he asked himself what love would do with a person who showed weakness: it would not humiliate her, but would try to lift her up and offer her a way out, not naively, but as **option B**.\n\nThe outcome was good: the money was returned, self-confidence was developed, and everyone moved to a new level because the reaction was not impulsive but wise. Salopek states that this is what corporations and individuals, saleswomen and managers need: **empathy, compassion and the strength not to react, but to remain in wisdom** and seek truth. When he does not know what the truth is, he advises asking what he would advise his own child, and then having the strength of love to carry it out in practice.\n\nThe host asks what happened with the other employee who „snitched“. Salopek replies that he personally „took down all the stars of the world“ for her. She showed great maturity because she understood that there is no „us“ but that there is responsibility, and she told him out of the greatest love. He promised that he would react wisely and thoughtfully. In the end both remained friends, and he solved a situation that he did not create.",

    {
     "subtitle": "The right to work, not to the result: what we can actually control",
     "screenshot_description": "Zoran Salopek explains the principle „you have the right to work, and you do not have the right to the result“.",
